name: Emeka Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What's a normal day on the phones like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the later water-billing shift at Northline. People ring when they get home and open a bill, and I read meter numbers back slowly before changing anything. The late hours carry a premium that Salma, my partner, and I have built our rent budget around.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Password resets, mostly; there are dozens that sound the same. I've been here long enough to know the recurring billing errors, but I'm not a supervisor. I write disputed readings on paper because I don't use the new AI draft tool.

say: I would welcome **quicker paperwork** while checking disputed meter readings myself.
I would ask the **union branch** to watch paid late-shift hours.
think: I expect my **billing pay** to hold in this mild change.
I need **verified later income** before reducing paid work.
do: Keep taking **evening billing calls** and checking readings on paper.
Compare **annual earnings** with rent and bills alongside Salma.
feel: **Calm** about current work, with a quiet later-income question.
S0.quote: A neat answer is no use when the meter number is wrong.
fieldNote: His nine-month **reserve** is not lifelong income.
He trusts **paper readings** more than AI drafts for disputes.
His secondary school background and resistance to AI leave **paper checks** central to his sense of competence.

steps.text: Keep evening water-billing calls and check disputed meter readings on paper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that quicker paperwork is fine if we still check meter numbers ourselves. A neat answer is no use when the meter number is wrong. I'd ask the union branch to watch the late rota, even in a quiet year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work and pay hold up in this picture. We have about nine months of expenses saved, but I have not checked what income would replace my wage if I stopped full-time work. Mild AI doesn't answer that question for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking evening calls and checking disputed readings on paper. This year I'd get our actual annual earnings from payroll and compare them with rent and bills alongside Salma. In the first year of this picture I'd keep the same rota while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, mostly. Later-life money stays in the back of my head, but it isn't keeping me awake this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you do with the earnings figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma and I would see what a shorter week really costs us. We won't call nine months saved a lifelong income. If the figures don't work, I'd carry on with paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children the water line is steady and we aren't asking them to cover our bills. They have their own households. I don't want a quiet change at work turned into a family alarm.

I would press for **written hours** before late shifts are cut.
think: Routine AI answers could shrink my **premium hours**.
My **reserve** buys time, though lower pay changes our rent budget.
do: Record disputed calls where the **AI draft** gets the reading wrong.
Join late-shift agents in a **union request** for review time and paid hours.
Cancel the **streaming bundle** only if premium hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible premium cut, with some control through colleagues.
S1.quote: A job title does not pay the rent if the premium hours disappear.
fieldNote: His concern is **paid hours**, even if his title survives.
The union request is **shared action** with three other late-shift agents.
He names **streaming** as a cut only after actual premium income falls, rather than cutting in anticipation.

steps.text: Keep paid evening calls and record wrong meter-reading drafts
Join late-shift agents and union branch seeking written review time and paid hours
Cancel monthly streaming bundle only if premium hours actually fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask colleagues to log cases where a draft closes a bill before a person checks the meter. Three late-shift agents and I would bring those examples to the union branch to ask for human review time. I don't want faster answers used to strip the late rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Northline could replace routine calls and trim my premium hours. A job title does not pay the rent if the premium hours disappear. Nine months saved buys time, but Salma and I would have to recalculate the weekly budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd record disputed calls where the generated answer is wrong. I'd join the other late-shift agents in asking the union branch for written paid hours and human checking time. If my premium hours actually fall over the next few years, we'd cancel the monthly streaming bundle; in the first year of the change I'd keep paid calls while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because losing the premium is a real income loss even if I still wear the headset. I can organise with others and look at the rota, which gives me something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the streaming bundle go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when the rota shows less money coming home, not because of a headline. The streaming bundle is our first optional payment. Rent and food aren't optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are the other agents willing to act with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring examples together and ask for a written reply on review time and paid hours. One person grumbling at the desk won't change a rota.

do: Join late-shift agents seeking **written closure dates** through the union.
Check **posted paid openings** by full-week wages.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected income loss and awake at night calculating the gap.
S2.quote: Nine months saved is a buffer, not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: He expects the **premium wage** to vanish with the calls.

steps.text: Join late-shift agents and union in demanding written closure dates and paid hours
Check posted depot and reception roles by full-week wages and rota
Apply if calls end in first year after 2028; accept only bill-covering paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the late shift that a cheap thinking system could take billing calls before we know where the next wage comes from. Robots arrive around 2031, but that's no extra time for a headset. I'd ask the union for closure dates and paid hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my Northline calls to go in the first year after 2028, and I'd lie awake over losing the premium. Nine months saved is a buffer, not a replacement wage. Other contact centres nearby may use the same cheap system, so their vacancies aren't guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join the late-shift group asking the union for written closure and paid-hour dates. I'd check posted paid openings at water depots and local reception desks by full-week wage and rota. If calls end after 2028, I'd apply for suitable paid work and use the reserve for rent while searching; I'd move only when actual hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can manage nine months of expenses, but I can't make a new wage appear on a deadline. I'd be awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why depots as well as other centres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot counter has people bringing in broken meters, so there may still be some paid work while physical tasks need people. I can't claim that lasts beyond robots around 2031. I'd check posted duties and pay instead of assuming a depot sign means safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use savings for rent only if paid calls stopped, not pour them into a course without a vacancy. Salma's canteen wage helps with food but doesn't replace my late-shift pay. I'd keep a monthly tally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch we have five years to ask which human checks Northline will still pay for. I want training tied to a real paid post, not a certificate that looks tidy in a drawer. I won't claim the depot is safe forever when robots may reach hands-on tasks around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me document disputes the machine gets wrong and show why a person still needs to check them. I still think most calls could go by 2031, taking my late premium. I can use savings to search, but I can't set a retirement date without knowing later income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd log recurring billing errors and join the union branch's request for posted paid review work. If offered, I'd ask to shadow a paid checker for two shifts before moving off my rota. In the first year after 2031, if calls fall, I'd apply to a posted review role only if its full paid week covers our bills; otherwise I'd keep any paid calls and search locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than sleepless now. Five years lets me put a case on paper and check a real rota. It still doesn't promise a wage at the other end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like the AI draft tool; would you use it in review work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read an AI answer after checking the source meter record myself, if that is what a paid review job asks. I don't need to build the system. My skill is explaining a wrong bill to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take a review post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two paid shadow shifts and a posted weekly rota would tell me more than a training leaflet. If losing the late premium puts pay below our bills, I'd keep paid calls while they exist and look elsewhere. Salma and I can absorb a little change, not an endless gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to argue for fair warning, not enough to promise everyone a safe job. I'd keep asking the union branch to publish rota figures each year. Robots arrive around 2039, but desk work changes in 2036 or earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still need paid work at sixty-eight; I haven't verified any income that would replace my wage. Nine months saved gives Salma and me search choices, not a date when bills stop. A long warning could tempt me to leave the figures until too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd put actual earnings and costs on one sheet and request written figures for any later-life income. I'd keep the late billing rota while it pays and join the union branch's yearly request for staffing dates. If calls end in the first year after 2036, I'd compare posted jobs by full-week wages and hours before moving, and keep working if verified later income won't cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened tonight. Ten years gives room to check facts, but it's not a paid plan by itself. I don't want my grown children thinking they must sort it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later-income figures are too small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep paid work in the plan and look for shifts I can manage. I might want shorter hours later, but only if Salma and I can see how rent gets paid every month. A birthday is not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you stop putting off the income check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the income check on the calendar with our yearly rent review. The union branch can ask for staffing dates each year, but I still have to read our own figures. No meeting can do that for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I could lose the late premium before another wage is ready. Written staffing dates and actual paid openings would help more than promises about learning something new. Nine months saved is useful, but it isn't a replacement wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the odd hours that make a modest job pay properly. My job title would look the same on paper if my employer Northline stripped the evening premium. Salma and I would notice it at the rent payment.

headlineQuote: My job title would look the same on paper if my employer Northline stripped the evening premium.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old** experienced water-billing agent with secondary school education.
He earns **higher pay** through late shifts and has nine months saved.
He **avoids AI tools** but checks disputed meter readings on paper.
His **union activity** focuses on written paid hours and human review.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when billing calls and the late premium may vanish before another wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates** and paid openings with complete weekly hours.
